subject: English
description: Words from Latin VERTERE/VERSUM (to turn): convert, divert, revert, pervert, invert, subvert, avert, versatile, universe, adverse, version — meanings, usage, and distinctions. High-frequency PYQ vocabulary.

options.option_text: Turn aside or redirect — traffic was diverted from the accident site
Return to a previous state — the patient diverted to his old diet after discharge
Undermine a system from below — activists sought to divert the government gradually
Turn completely opposite — the conclusion diverts everything the study assumed earlier

questions.explanation: DIVERT = DI/DIS (aside, away) + VERTERE (to turn) = to turn aside; redirect. USES: divert traffic, divert funds (redirect money from intended purpose — often implies misuse), divert attention (distract). RELATED FORMS: DIVERSION (the act of turning aside; also entertainment — a diversion from stress). COMPARE VERT FAMILY: REVERT = RE (back) + VERT = return to a previous state. SUBVERT = SUB (under) + VERT = undermine from below. INVERT = IN (inside, against) + VERT = turn upside down or reverse. AVERT = A/AB (away) + VERT = turn away (avert disaster = prevent by turning it away; avert your eyes = look away). DIVERT ≠ REVERT (option B) ≠ SUBVERT (option C) ≠ INVERT (option D). PYQ FREQUENCY: divert, revert, subvert usage in SSC CGL, IBPS PO vocabulary/fill-in-blank — 1-2× per year.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The sentence 'The company tried to revert back to its original pricing policy' contains a redundancy error. The error is:

options.option_text: 'revert back' — 'revert' already means to go back; 'back' is redundant
'tried to revert' — the infinitive form is wrong; 'reverted' should be used directly
'its original pricing policy' — should be 'their original pricing policy' for a company
No redundancy — 'revert back' adds emphasis and is accepted in standard written English

questions.explanation: REVERT = RE (back) + VERTERE (to turn) = to turn back; return to a previous condition. Since 'back' is BUILT INTO the meaning of 'revert,' adding 'back' creates a TAUTOLOGY (redundancy). CORRECT: 'The company tried to REVERT to its original pricing policy.' OTHER COMMON REDUNDANCIES WITH VERT ROOTS: 'RETURN back' (return = go back already). 'REPEAT again' (repeat = say again). 'RECOIL back' (recoil = spring back). REVERT USES: policies, systems, behaviour reverting to baseline; inheritance law (property reverts to the Crown if no heir); ecology (land reverting to wilderness). COMPANY PRONOUN: 'its pricing policy' is correct (company = singular entity in Indian/US English). PYQ FREQUENCY: revert vs revert back redundancy in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1× per year.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best fills the blank: 'The union leader was accused of trying to ________ the democratic process from within.'

options.option_text: Subvert — to undermine or overthrow from below (sub=under + vert=turn)
Convert — to change one's form or belief; does not imply undermining from within
Divert — to redirect; does not capture the sense of secret undermining of a system
Avert — to prevent or turn away; used for avoiding events, not for internal sabotage

questions.explanation: SUBVERT = SUB (under, secretly) + VERTERE (to turn) = to turn the foundations under something; to undermine or overthrow (especially a government, system, or established order) from within or secretly. CONTEXT CLUE: 'from within' + 'accused of' + 'democratic process' = classic subversion scenario. SUBVERSION: the act of subverting; subversive activities (in law and politics). SUBVERSIVE: an adjective or noun — a subversive element. COMPARE: DIVERT (redirect), CONVERT (change form — religion, currency, format), AVERT (prevent/avoid), INVERT (flip upside down). LEGAL ANGLE: Sedition and subversion are distinct legal concepts — subversion typically refers to attempts to overthrow/undermine; sedition to incitement. UPSC ANGLE: Art 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions on free speech for 'overthrowing the State' — subversion context. PYQ FREQUENCY: subvert in SSC CGL, IBPS PO fill-in-blank, UPSC CSAT 1× per 2 years.

questions.stem: A person described as 'VERSATILE' is one who:

options.option_text: Can turn to many different tasks or roles — capable of adapting to varied situations
Holds strong and unchanging opinions — firm in one position without turning or wavering
Frequently changes opinions without logic — a turncoat who shifts sides opportunistically
Has an inverted or unconventional way of thinking — often goes against the mainstream

questions.explanation: VERSATILE = VERS (to turn) + ATILE (suffix, capable of) = able to turn to many things; adaptable to many uses, roles, or subjects. ETYMOLOGY: from Latin VERSATILIS = turning easily. USES: 'a versatile actor' (can play many genres); 'a versatile tool' (many functions); 'a versatile player' (can play multiple positions). VERSATILITY (noun). EXAM TRAP: Option C (changes opinions) sounds like versatile but describes an OPPORTUNIST or TURNCOAT — not a positive quality. Versatile = positively adaptable; turncoat = negatively unprincipled. UNIVERS-E: same root — UNIVERSE = UNUS (one) + VERTERE (turned into one) = all things turned/combined into one whole. ANNIVERSARY: ANNUS (year) + VERTERE (turn) = the year turning around. UNIVERSE, ANNIVERSARY, VERSATILE — all from VERTERE. PYQ FREQUENCY: versatile in SSC CGL vocabulary, IBPS PO synonym/antonym questions — 1× per year.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The words AVERT and DIVERT both come from VERT. Which sentence correctly uses 'AVERT' (not 'divert')?

options.option_text: Quick action by the pilot averted a mid-air collision over the city airport last week
The authorities averted the traffic to an alternate route during the waterlogging
The coach averted the team's attention towards their defensive weaknesses overall
The government averted funds from infrastructure to emergency relief spending

questions.explanation: AVERT = A/AB (away) + VERTERE (turn) = to turn away; specifically to PREVENT something undesirable from happening or to look away. USE: 'avert a disaster,' 'avert a crisis,' 'avert one's gaze.' DIVERT = to redirect or turn aside something that is ongoing. ANALYSIS: Option A — 'averted a collision' = prevented (turned away from) a collision ✓. Option B — 'averted the traffic to an alternate route' is WRONG; this is DIVERTING (redirecting) traffic, not averting it. Option C — 'averted the team's attention' is WRONG; this is DIVERTING attention (turning it aside), not averting. Option D — 'averted funds' is WRONG; this is DIVERTING funds. MEMORY: AVERT = A(void) + VERT = turn away/prevent (disaster/crisis). DIVERT = redirect what's flowing. PYQ FREQUENCY: avert vs divert distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO fill-in-blank — 1× per year.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'The court issued an adverse ruling against the company,' the word 'adverse' most precisely means:

options.option_text: Unfavourable; turned against — AD (toward) + VERSUS (turned against) = directed against
Excessively critical in tone — an adverse ruling is harsh and unnecessarily punitive
Unexpected and sudden — an adverse ruling catches the defendant by complete surprise
Preliminary or interim — an adverse ruling is not yet final pending further appeal

questions.explanation: ADVERSE = AD (toward) + VERSUS (turned) = turned toward (in opposition); unfavourable, harmful, opposing. ETYMOLOGY: from ADVERSUS (turned against, opposite). USES: adverse conditions (unfavourable conditions), adverse effects (harmful side effects), adverse ruling (ruling going against you), adverse possession (legal term: occupying another's land adversely). ADVERSE vs AVERSE: AVERSE = turned away from (reluctant, disinclined — 'I am not averse to the idea'). ADVERSE = working against, unfavourable. EXAM TRAP: adverse and averse are frequently confused. AVERSE relates to personal reluctance; ADVERSE relates to external unfavourable forces. VERSUS: from same root — used in legal/sports contexts to mean 'against' (Company A versus Company B). ADVERSARY: an opponent (from ADVERSARIUS — one who turns against you). PYQ FREQUENCY: adverse vs averse distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO vocabulary — 1-2× per year.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Which of the following words does NOT come from the Latin root VERTERE (to turn)?

options.option_text: Revert, Subvert, Universe, Versatile, Adverse — all from VERTERE; none is the odd one out
PERVERT — per (through) + vert (turn) = to turn thoroughly/distort; IS from VERTERE
TRAVERSE — trans (across) + vers (turn) = to cross or go across; also from VERTERE
CONVERT, DIVERT, INVERT, AVERT — all from VERTERE; VERTIGO is from VERTIGINEM (turning/dizziness)

questions.explanation: ALL listed words except this question's trick stem from VERTERE. The question is formatted to check comprehension of the root. FULL VERTERE FAMILY: CONVERT (con+vert = change together), DIVERT (di+vert = turn aside), REVERT (re+vert = turn back), INVERT (in+vert = turn inside/upside down), SUBVERT (sub+vert = turn from under), AVERT (ab+vert = turn away), PERVERT (per+vert = turn completely/distort), TRAVERSE (trans+vers = cross), VERSATILE (vers+atile = able to turn to many things), ADVERSE (ad+versus = turned against), UNIVERSE (uni+versus = turned into one), ANNIVERSARY (anni+versus = year-turn), CONTROVERSY (contra+versus = turned against = debate), VERSION (a turning/rendering of text). VERTIGO: from Latin VERTIGINEM (a whirling) = dizziness — also from VERTERE but often listed separately. MEMORY AID: if the word has VER-, VERS-, or VERT- inside it, suspect VERTERE. PYQ FREQUENCY: root identification across words in CAT verbal, SSC CGL, IBPS PO — 1× per 2-3 years.
